# What we are doing

A hierarchical model lets thirty series share information: each gets its own effect, drawn from a
common distribution the data also estimates. Data-poor series borrow from data-rich ones, and
nobody has to choose the weights.

That is genuinely powerful, and today you will watch it work. You will also watch it produce a
confidently wrong answer — on the same data, with clean diagnostics, textbook shrinkage, and no
warning of any kind.

The difference between the two runs is not the code. It is a decision made before any code was
written: **which series belong in the same hierarchy.**

**Suggested time:** ~45 minutes · **You will need:** `pandas`, `numpy`, `matplotlib`, `pymc`, `arviz`, and
`data/processed/m5_weekly.csv`. Five model fits, most under 30 seconds.

---

# Setup

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pymc as pm
import arviz as az
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
RANDOM_STATE = 42

weekly = pd.read_csv("../data/processed/m5_weekly.csv", parse_dates=["week_start"])
weekly["series"] = weekly.store_id + "_" + weekly.cat_id
weekly["hi_snap"] = (weekly.snap_days >= 5).astype(int)

df = weekly.dropna(subset=["units"]).copy()
df["ly"] = np.log(df.units.clip(lower=1))

print(f"{df.series.nunique()} series | {len(df):,} rows | "
      f"{df.hi_snap.mean():.1%} of weeks are high-SNAP")
```

Our question: **does a high-SNAP week lift units, and by how much in each store?**

We will need one helper repeatedly — the SNAP effect actually observed in a set of weeks, with
no model involved. It is just the difference in mean log units between high-SNAP weeks and the
rest.

```{python}
def empirical_effect(frame, series_name):
    """Observed high-SNAP effect on log units for one series."""
    z = frame[frame.series == series_name]
    if z.hi_snap.nunique() < 2:
        return np.nan
    return z.ly[z.hi_snap == 1].mean() - z.ly[z.hi_snap == 0].mean()
```

---

# Step 1 — Build the imbalance

Real panels are lopsided: some series have years of history, others are new stores or newly
re-categorized products with a handful of usable weeks. We create that imbalance deliberately so
we can check the answer later.

Thin every third series down to 8 weeks. The weeks we remove are not thrown away — they become a
held-out set that the model never sees, and that we will use in Step 3 to grade it.

```{python}
codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df.series)
df["idx"] = codes
J = len(uniq)

rng = np.random.RandomState(RANDOM_STATE)
keep = []
for j in range(J):
    rows = df.index[df.idx == j].tolist()
    n = 8 if j % 3 == 0 else len(rows)
    keep += list(rng.choice(rows, size=min(n, len(rows)), replace=False))

train = df.loc[sorted(keep)].copy()
heldout = df.drop(index=keep).copy()
thin = np.array([j % 3 == 0 for j in range(J)])

print(f"train {len(train):,} rows | held-out {len(heldout):,} rows")
print(f"{thin.sum()} thin series (8 weeks each), {(~thin).sum()} full series")
```

Here is the model. It is the one from lecture, written non-centered, and it takes a flag so we can
reuse it for the unpooled fit.

```{python}
def fit(data, kind, n_series, centered=False, target_accept=0.9):
    """kind: 'unpooled' or 'hier'. Returns the InferenceData."""
    i = data.idx.values
    x = data.hi_snap.values.astype(float)
    y = data.ly.values
    with pm.Model():
        a = pm.Normal("a", y.mean(), 1, shape=n_series)
        s = pm.Exponential("s", 1.0)
        if kind == "unpooled":
            b = pm.Normal("b", 0, 0.5, shape=n_series)
        else:
            mu_b = pm.Normal("mu_b", 0, 0.5)
            sd_b = pm.HalfNormal("sd_b", 0.25)
            if centered:
                b = pm.Normal("b", mu_b, sd_b, shape=n_series)
            else:
                z = pm.Normal("z", 0, 1, shape=n_series)
                b = pm.Deterministic("b", mu_b + z * sd_b)
        pm.Normal("obs", mu=a[i] + b[i] * x, sigma=s, observed=y)
        return pm.sample(1000, tune=1500, chains=4, progressbar=False,
                         random_seed=RANDOM_STATE, target_accept=target_accept)

def b_means(idata, n_series):
    return az.summary(idata, var_names=["b"], ci_kind="hdi",
                      ci_prob=0.94)["mean"].values
```

---

# Step 2 — Fit it, and admire the shrinkage

Fit both models on all thirty series and measure how far each estimate moved.

```{python}
idata_u30 = fit(train, "unpooled", J)
idata_h30 = fit(train, "hier", J)

bu30, bh30 = b_means(idata_u30, J), b_means(idata_h30, J)

def diag(idata, label):
    su = az.summary(idata, var_names=["b"], ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94)
    print(f"  {label:<14s} r_hat {su.r_hat.max():.3f}  "
          f"ess {su.ess_bulk.min():5.0f}  "
          f"divergences {int(idata.sample_stats.diverging.sum()):4d}")

print("Diagnostics")
diag(idata_u30, "unpooled")
diag(idata_h30, "hierarchical")
```

```{python}
move_thin = np.abs(bh30[thin] - bu30[thin]).mean()
move_full = np.abs(bh30[~thin] - bu30[~thin]).mean()

print("\n              unpooled spread   after pooling   mean move")
print(f"  thin (8w)       {bu30[thin].std():.3f}           "
      f"{bh30[thin].std():.3f}          {move_thin:.3f}")
print(f"  full (277w)     {bu30[~thin].std():.3f}           "
      f"{bh30[~thin].std():.3f}          {move_full:.3f}")
print(f"\n  ratio: thin series moved {move_thin / move_full:.1f}x further")

g = az.summary(idata_h30, var_names=["mu_b", "sd_b"], ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94)
print(f"  mu_b {g.loc['mu_b','mean']:.3f}   sd_b {g.loc['sd_b','mean']:.3f}")
```

Everything a hierarchical model is supposed to do, it did. Diagnostics are clean. The data-poor
series moved an order of magnitude further toward the group mean than the data-rich ones, and
nobody told the model which was which.

The shrinkage plot makes it visual.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Each line is one series, before and after pooling."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
for j in range(J):
    c = "crimson" if thin[j] else "steelblue"
    ax.plot([0, 1], [bu30[j], bh30[j]], "-o", color=c, alpha=0.7, ms=4)
ax.axhline(g.loc["mu_b", "mean"], ls="--", c="gray", lw=1)
ax.set_xticks([0, 1]); ax.set_xticklabels(["unpooled", "hierarchical"])
ax.set_ylabel("estimated high-SNAP effect (log units)")
ax.set_title("Shrinkage: thin series (red) collapse onto the group mean")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Before you go on

Write down, in one sentence, what you would now tell the business. Keep it — Step 3 will ask
whether it was right.

# Step 3 — Grade it against the weeks it never saw

We thinned those ten series ourselves. The weeks we removed are sitting in `heldout`, and each
thinned series has hundreds of them. So we can compute the effect that *actually* occurred and
compare.

```{python}
thin_names = [uniq[j] for j in range(J) if thin[j]]
truth = np.array([empirical_effect(heldout, s) for s in thin_names])
est_u = np.array([bu30[j] for j in range(J) if thin[j]])
est_h = np.array([bh30[j] for j in range(J) if thin[j]])

out = pd.DataFrame({"series": thin_names, "unpooled": est_u.round(3),
                    "hierarchical": est_h.round(3), "held_out_truth": truth.round(3)})
print(out.to_string(index=False))

rmse = lambda e: np.sqrt(np.nanmean((e - truth) ** 2))
print(f"\n  RMSE vs truth:  unpooled {rmse(est_u):.3f}   "
      f"hierarchical {rmse(est_h):.3f}")
print(f"  mean held-out effect across these series: {np.nanmean(truth):.3f}")
```

Read that table before reading on.

The hierarchical model reported an effect near `mu_b` for every one of these series. The held-out
weeks say the true effects average close to 0.09 — several times larger. The model did not merely
lose precision on these series; it moved them all to the wrong place, and reported tight
intervals around it.

And notice what the RMSE column says: pooling barely improved on the unpooled fit at all. All
that shrinkage bought us essentially nothing.

::: {.callout-important}
## The diagnostics could never have caught this

$\hat{R}$, ESS and divergences ask whether the sampler explored the posterior of *the model you
wrote*. They cannot ask whether that model was the right one. Every diagnostic here passed.
:::

---

# Step 4 — Find out what went wrong

Two things are wrong, and one of them is invisible until you look.

First, look at which series we thinned.

```{python}
print("thinned series:", thin_names)
```

```{python}
print("\nEmpirical high-SNAP effect by category (all data, no model):")
for cat, grp in df.groupby("cat_id"):
    effs = [empirical_effect(grp, s) for s in grp.series.unique()]
    print(f"  {cat:<10s} n={len(effs):2d}  mean {np.mean(effs):+.3f}  "
          f"sd {np.std(effs):.3f}")
```

Two findings, and they compound.

**The groups were not exchangeable.** SNAP is a *food* assistance program. FOODS responds;
HOBBIES and HOUSEHOLD barely move. Putting all thirty in one hierarchy told the model these are
thirty interchangeable draws from one distribution — so it estimated a group mean near zero,
dominated by the twenty series with no effect, and pulled the FOODS series down to it.

**And `j % 3 == 0` selected exactly the FOODS series.** The series are ordered store-major with
three categories each, so every third one is a FOODS series. We starved precisely the ten series
that had something to say, then pooled them toward twenty that did not.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Exchangeability is a modeling assumption, and it is yours to defend

Groups are exchangeable when, before seeing the data, you have no reason to expect one to differ
from another in a particular direction. Ten FOODS series in ten stores: plausible. FOODS against
HOBBIES: you knew the answer before you looked.

Nothing in PyMC checks this. No diagnostic reports it. It is subject-matter knowledge, applied
before the model is written.
:::

# Step 5 — Do it on the exchangeable set

Restrict to the ten FOODS series — the set we can actually defend pooling — and rebuild the same
imbalance: thin every other one to 8 weeks.

```{python}
foods = df[df.cat_id == "FOODS"].copy()
codes_f, uniq_f = pd.factorize(foods.series)
foods["idx"] = codes_f
Jf = len(uniq_f)

rng = np.random.RandomState(RANDOM_STATE)
keep_f = []
for j in range(Jf):
    rows = foods.index[foods.idx == j].tolist()
    n = 8 if j % 2 == 0 else len(rows)
    keep_f += list(rng.choice(rows, size=min(n, len(rows)), replace=False))

train_f = foods.loc[sorted(keep_f)].copy()
heldout_f = foods.drop(index=keep_f).copy()
thin_f = np.array([j % 2 == 0 for j in range(Jf)])

print(f"{Jf} FOODS series | {thin_f.sum()} thinned to 8 weeks")
print(f"train {len(train_f):,} rows | held-out {len(heldout_f):,} rows")
```

```{python}
idata_uf = fit(train_f, "unpooled", Jf)
idata_hf = fit(train_f, "hier", Jf)
buf, bhf = b_means(idata_uf, Jf), b_means(idata_hf, Jf)

gf = az.summary(idata_hf, var_names=["mu_b", "sd_b"], ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94)
print(gf.round(3).to_string())
```

```{python}
mt = np.abs(bhf[thin_f] - buf[thin_f]).mean()
mf = np.abs(bhf[~thin_f] - buf[~thin_f]).mean()
print("              unpooled spread   after pooling   mean move")
print(f"  thin (8w)       {buf[thin_f].std():.3f}           "
      f"{bhf[thin_f].std():.3f}          {mt:.3f}")
print(f"  full (277w)     {buf[~thin_f].std():.3f}           "
      f"{bhf[~thin_f].std():.3f}          {mf:.3f}")
print(f"\n  ratio: thin moved {mt / mf:.1f}x further")
```

Compare that middle column to Step 2's. There, *everything* collapsed onto the group mean. Here
the thin series collapse but the full series **keep most of their spread** — the model discarded
variation that 8 weeks could not support and kept variation that 277 weeks could. That is what
partial pooling is supposed to look like.

Now grade it the same way.

```{python}
tn = [uniq_f[j] for j in range(Jf) if thin_f[j]]
truth_f = np.array([empirical_effect(heldout_f, s) for s in tn])
eu = np.array([buf[j] for j in range(Jf) if thin_f[j]])
eh = np.array([bhf[j] for j in range(Jf) if thin_f[j]])

print(pd.DataFrame({"series": tn, "unpooled": eu.round(3),
                    "hierarchical": eh.round(3),
                    "held_out_truth": truth_f.round(3)}).to_string(index=False))

r_u = np.sqrt(np.nanmean((eu - truth_f) ** 2))
r_h = np.sqrt(np.nanmean((eh - truth_f) ** 2))
print(f"\n  RMSE vs truth:  unpooled {r_u:.3f}   hierarchical {r_h:.3f}"
      f"   ({r_u / r_h:.1f}x better)")
```

**That is borrowing strength, and now it is real.** The same code, the same priors, the same
diagnostics — and the thin series are estimated well because the other five exist. The only thing
that changed was which series were allowed into the hierarchy.

# Step 6 — The trap in the code

One more failure, and this one *is* mechanical. The natural way to write the hierarchy reads
exactly like the equation:

```python
b = pm.Normal("b", mu_b, sd_b, shape=J)   # the centered form
```

Fit it that way and watch the diagnostics.

```{python}
idata_cent = fit(train_f, "hier", Jf, centered=True)

print("Diagnostics")
diag(idata_cent, "centered")
diag(idata_hf, "non-centered")
```

Same model. Same data. Same answer, if you could sample it — but the centered form makes the
sampler walk a funnel: when `sd_b` is small the `b_j` must crowd into a narrow neck, and a
sampler tuned for the wide part cannot get in.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Which alarm fired

Look at the two columns. $\hat{R}$ passes and ESS clears 400 — on those two numbers alone you
would have shipped it. The divergence count is unambiguous.

Your count may not match a classmate's: divergence counts move with the seed, and even with the
machine. The pattern should not move — the centered form diverges, the non-centered form barely or
not at all.

On hierarchical models, divergences are the sensitive instrument. Do not wait for $\hat{R}$.
:::
